abstract: Dr. Ledbetter discusses the use of point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) for diagnosing and managing abscesses, emphasizing that ultrasound reduces the failure rate of incision from 17% (physical exam alone) to 3.7%. The lecture covers probe selection (linear probe for superficial abscesses), scanning technique (two planes, entire area), and key sonographic findings including cobblestoning (fluid in subcutaneous tissue, seen in both cellulitis and edema) and abscess characteristics (anechoic or heterogeneous, with possible septations). It also highlights the importance of Doppler to distinguish abscess from vessels or lymph nodes, and demonstrates utility for foreign body detection and marking.
key_points: Ultrasound plus physical exam reduces abscess incision failure rate from 17% to 3.7%.
Use a linear probe for superficial abscesses; scan the entire area of concern in two planes.
Cobblestoning indicates fluid in subcutaneous tissue but cannot differentiate cellulitis from edema without clinical context.
Abscesses may be anechoic, hypoechoic, or heterogeneous; septations suggest need for open drainage rather than needle aspiration.
Doppler is essential to confirm an abscess is not a blood vessel and to identify nearby vessels before incision.
Lymph nodes can mimic abscesses; look for a central hilum with Doppler flow to avoid cutting into them.
Ultrasound effectively detects foreign bodies (splinters, glass, metal) and can guide removal, especially with a water bath technique.
Measure abscess in three dimensions (depth, width, length) by rotating the probe 90 degrees.
Compressibility and movement of fluid ("hustle stalsis") help identify isoechoic abscesses.
Probe safety: keep water level below the gasket; confirm with attending before submerging.
